title: The Pali Text Society
hookLine: founded 1881 to publish the texts; the translations we read here began there
last: A GOOD MAN PERVADES EVERY PLACE.

cards: Look under the quotations on this path and two names keep turning up. Max Müller, for the Dhammapada. And Rhys Davids, for the suttas.
"Thus have I heard." The Buddha's last words. The advice to be a lamp to yourself.

Those English sentences came to us through Rhys Davids' hands and the hands of the people he worked with. Behind them stands an unlikely thing: a society, set up in London by scholars, with a plain goal.
Print the Pali texts so anyone could read them, and put them into English.

teach.b: We met T. W. Rhys Davids a few days back, among the first translators.
He had worked in Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, as a British official. Accounts say he first learned Pali there, from a Sri Lankan monk, so he could read old documents in court.
He came home wanting the texts he had met to be open to everyone.

teach.h: A SOCIETY TO PRINT THE TEXTS.
teach.b: So he founded the Pali Text Society, to edit the Pali texts and print them in roman letters.
Before that, they lived mainly in palm-leaf manuscripts in monasteries in Sri Lanka, Burma and Thailand, in local scripts. The work was never one person's.
Scholars in Europe and Asia edited texts side by side, comparing manuscripts.
Monks in Asia lent manuscripts and answered questions. Caroline Rhys Davids, his wife, translated and edited, and later led the society herself. Then came translations.
Rhys Davids' Dialogues of the Buddha opens its first sutta with: "Thus have I heard."

Every translation is a set of choices, and later translators have made different ones. The society still publishes, and scholars still find their way around the Pali texts by the volume and page numbers of its editions.
Here, we read what the translators handed us.

how: Students and scholars of the Pali tradition read and cite the texts in the editions and translations of the Pali Text Society, alongside newer translations, and monasteries keep chanting the texts in Pali.

practice: Bring to mind one line from this path that stayed with you, thus have I heard, maybe, or a verse of the Dhammapada, and think back along the chain it traveled: the monks who memorized it, the scribes who wrote it on palm leaves, the editors who compared copies, the translators who chose each English word.
You don't know most of their names; silently, thank them anyway. Then rest with the line itself.
